title: Sabbath vs Sunday
closing: I showed thee a meeting and a warning. I did not show thee a command to change the day.

romanScripture.quote: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God

exchanges.claim: I grant Exodus names the seventh day. But isn't the lasting principle one day in seven, with the day itself adaptable?

choices.argument: The creation account emphasizes God's rest, so I'd carry over the rhythm and leave the choice of day open.

scripture.quote: he rested on the seventh day from all his work

choices.feedback: The rest explains the rhythm, but the next verse blesses a named day. The excerpt supplies no basis for leaving the day open.

choices.argument: The rhythm matters, but Genesis blesses the seventh day itself. Exodus keeps that same day in the command.

scripture.quote: And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it

choices.feedback: Genesis blesses a particular day. Exodus carries that specificity into the command.

exchanges.explanation: Exodus uses the creation pattern to explain why the seventh day was blessed. A transferable principle is an application beyond the wording.
exchanges.editorialNotes: Distinguish the day named in the command from debates about later covenant application.

romanScripture.quote: The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath

exchanges.claim: Fair. But if the Sabbath serves people, why couldn't Yeshua's disciples adapt the day to their needs?

choices.argument: Yeshua brings up David's hunger because the dispute is over what they did that day, not which day to keep.

scripture.quote: when he had need, and was an hungred

choices.feedback: David's need answers the charge over the disciples' conduct on the Sabbath already in view.

choices.argument: If Yeshua is Lord of the Sabbath, his disciples can adapt the day when their mission calls for it.

scripture.quote: Therefore the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath.

choices.feedback: His authority is explicit. The passage never says he delegated authority to change the day to his disciples.

exchanges.explanation: Yeshua invokes David's hunger and claims authority over the Sabbath. His response concerns what happened on the day already being observed.
exchanges.editorialNotes: Readers differ on the wider scope of his authority here. Grade the action and conclusion shown in this scene.

romanScripture.quote: Now upon the first day of the week, very early in the morning, they came unto the sepulchre

exchanges.claim: Then let's look beyond the grainfields. The first-day visit marks the discovery of the resurrection. Isn't that reason to make it the new Sabbath?

choices.argument: The empty tomb gives us a reason to celebrate, but Luke puts the commanded rest before that first-day visit.

scripture.quote: rested the sabbath day according to the commandment.

choices.feedback: Luke connects the earlier rest to the commandment. The first-day visit is a separate event.

choices.argument: The resurrection is central enough that the day the women heard the news should become the church's weekly rest day.

scripture.quote: He is not here, but is risen

choices.feedback: The announcement supports celebration. It gives no weekly rest instruction and does not say the earlier Sabbath was replaced.

exchanges.explanation: Luke connects the women's rest to the commandment before reporting the visit. The narrative supplies two distinct events and does not prescribe a replacement day.
exchanges.editorialNotes: The passage dates the visit. Do not infer an exact resurrection hour or dismiss first-day commemoration.

romanScripture.quote: And upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached unto them

exchanges.claim: All right, the tomb account records an event. At Troas, though, the disciples actually gather and break bread. Why isn't that a weekly pattern?

choices.argument: Breaking bread was already a regular practice, so the first-day meeting at Troas gives us their normal weekly schedule.

scripture.quote: fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.

choices.feedback: Acts 2 supports regular fellowship and breaking bread without naming a weekday. One dated meeting does not establish a schedule.

choices.argument: They really did meet that day, but Paul was leaving the next day. Luke gives no rule for future gatherings.

scripture.quote: Paul preached unto them, ready to depart on the morrow

choices.feedback: Paul's departure gives the meeting its setting. Luke reports this gathering without prescribing a weekly schedule.

exchanges.explanation: Paul was preparing to leave, and Luke describes the events of that meeting. The passage records the gathering without prescribing a new rest day.
exchanges.editorialNotes: The nature of breaking bread and ancient day boundaries need not be settled to answer this claim.

romanScripture.quote: Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store

exchanges.claim: A meeting could be incidental. Paul gave Corinth and Galatia a first-day instruction, though. Doesn't that show a settled weekly practice?

choices.argument: Paul tells everyone to set something aside on the first day, so the gifts point to a regular church gathering.

scripture.quote: let every one of you lay by him in store

choices.feedback: The verse says what each person should do and when. It does not give a meeting as the setting.

choices.argument: Corinth and Galatia got the same instruction about gifts for the saints. That tells us what the schedule was for.

scripture.quote: Now concerning the collection for the saints

choices.feedback: Paul identifies the subject before specifying the day. The schedule concerns the collection.

exchanges.explanation: The order concerns a collection for the saints, with the gifts prepared before Paul arrives. The first-day timing is explicit. A required assembly is an inference.
exchanges.editorialNotes: Do not treat the location of the set-aside as settled by the wording.

chains.title: The Lord's day, judgment, and rest

romanScripture.quote: I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day

exchanges.claim: I'll grant the collection has its own purpose. But John uses a title his readers would recognize. Why wouldn't the Lord's day mean Sunday?

choices.argument: John locates his vision on the Lord's day. He gives the day a title but never names its weekday.

scripture.quote: I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day

choices.feedback: John gives a title and describes the vision. The line supplies no weekday or weekly rest command.

choices.argument: Yeshua calls himself Lord of the Sabbath, so I'd take John's title as a definite reference to the seventh day.

scripture.quote: Therefore the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath.

choices.feedback: Mark establishes Yeshua's authority over Sabbath. It does not define John's phrase in a different passage.

exchanges.explanation: John reports when he was in the Spirit without specifying a weekday. An identification with Sunday, Sabbath, or a prophetic day needs evidence beyond the line.
exchanges.editorialNotes: Editorial review should ensure the key addresses what the text establishes, rather than grading a particular historical identification.

romanScripture.quote: One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike.

exchanges.claim: Even if John doesn't settle the weekday, Paul lets believers regard days differently. Why would Sabbath be exempt from that freedom?

choices.argument: Paul tells believers to stop judging each other, so I would treat every weekly observance as a personal choice.

scripture.quote: Let us not therefore judge one another any more

choices.feedback: The instruction concerns how believers treat one another. It does not by itself identify every weekly observance as optional.

choices.argument: Paul puts different ways of regarding days alongside eating. He leaves the day unnamed, so the Sabbath application needs another step.

scripture.quote: He that regardeth the day, regardeth it unto the Lord

choices.feedback: Paul describes honoring the day alongside eating unto the Lord. The statement names no specific observance.

exchanges.explanation: Paul discusses days and eating while warning against judging fellow believers. He names no particular observance in these verses.
exchanges.editorialNotes: The range of days in Romans 14 is disputed. The key should remain a claim about the text's scope.

romanScripture.quote: Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days

exchanges.claim: Romans doesn't name it, but Colossians does. If Sabbath belongs with shadows fulfilled in Christ, why keep it as an obligation?

choices.argument: Paul calls these observances shadows, and his instruction is about judgment. He doesn't tell anyone to stop observing the Sabbath.

scripture.quote: Let no man therefore judge you

choices.feedback: Paul's direct instruction forbids judgment over the listed matters. A ban on observance requires a further argument.

choices.argument: Since the shadow points to Christ, I'd take keeping the weekly Sabbath as an obligation Paul expects believers to leave behind.

scripture.quote: Which are a shadow of things to come

choices.feedback: The image points to Christ, but it does not expressly forbid the practice. Paul's stated instruction addresses judgment.

exchanges.explanation: Paul's direct instruction forbids judgment over the listed practices. The shadow language relates them to Christ without issuing a ban on keeping Sabbath.
exchanges.editorialNotes: Review weekly versus festival scope and the force of the shadow image. The answer need not settle either.

romanScripture.quote: There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.

exchanges.claim: Granted, Colossians isn't a ban. But Hebrews says a rest remains for believers. Isn't that the rest the weekly Sabbath was pointing toward?

choices.argument: Hebrews brings God's seventh-day rest into the argument about entering his rest. It never says that entering it cancels the weekly day.

scripture.quote: And God did rest the seventh day from all his works.

choices.feedback: The creation reference links the themes. Hebrews urges entry into the promised rest without giving a weekly calendar change.

choices.argument: Hebrews urges believers to enter God's rest, so that promise takes over the role the weekly Sabbath used to serve.

scripture.quote: Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest

choices.feedback: The exhortation concerns entering the promised rest. It does not say the promise replaces weekly observance.

exchanges.explanation: Hebrews uses God's seventh-day rest in its argument about entering the rest that remains. It urges entry and does not state a change of weekly day.
exchanges.editorialNotes: The meaning of the remaining rest is debated. The strongest option allows a wider meaning while answering the implied replacement.

romanScripture.quote: And upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread

exchanges.claim: Put Troas together with Colossians. A first-day gathering and freedom from judgment over Sabbaths seem like grounds for calling Sunday the new Sabbath.

choices.argument: The disciples gathered on the first day, and Paul warned against judgment. That gives churches room to call Sunday their Sabbath.

scripture.quote: in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days

choices.feedback: A precedent for gathering and a warning against judgment may inform practice. Neither makes the gathering day take over the commandment.

choices.argument: Troas shows a meeting, and Colossians addresses judgment. Neither changes the seventh day Exodus actually names as the Sabbath.

scripture.quote: the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God

choices.feedback: Exodus names the day. A meeting and a warning against judgment do not together state a transfer of Sabbath rest.

exchanges.explanation: Acts describes a gathering and Colossians forbids judgment over the listed observances. Neither gives a command changing the seventh day named in Exodus.
exchanges.editorialNotes: Review whether the alternative clearly claims authority to call Sunday the Sabbath. A narrower claim about permission to gather on Sunday would be defensible.
